beats.narration_text: This tool has flagged sixteen contradictions between two AI agents. None of them were real. Not probably wrong. Not needs review. I turned all thirty-one runs this thing has ever stored into a labeled corpus. I replayed every one of them through today's code. I counted. Sixteen false positives. Zero cases of two agents citing different values for the same fact. The one time it did catch something real was a number an agent invented. The fix I shipped to reduce the false positives now suppresses that catch too. That's this week. Not a feature. A measurement.

props.command: What does replaying every stored run against today's code actually show?
output: Sixteen flagged runs, replayed against today's comparator, all sixteen
Zero of them are two agents citing different values for the same fact
The one confirmed catch this tool ever made doesn't flag anymore

beats.narration_text: Quick recap. Cross-Agent Validation compares two agents' conclusions about the same company. It flags mismatched numbers. It runs on an accountability layer. Storage is append-only, one record per attempt. The last video disclosed one limitation. It over-flags. Seven of twelve tickers came back flagged. The reason was never measured. The project's own words describe a second gap. Web static index dot html and app dot js are, as of that document, completely unmodified. Four sessions this period closed both gaps. They restructured the code. They measured the guess.

beats.act: chapter 2 - an interface that leads with its failures
beats.narration_text: The ask was specific. Don't demo the happy path. Show what's actually tested, and what's actually going wrong. So the first new module isn't a view. It's self_report dot py, a single source of truth for what's broken. Every issue carries a status. The test count is computed live, by unittest discovery. That's unlike the README's old claim of a hundred forty-three tests, wrong in three places. The warning above the compare button is generated from that ledger. It isn't hard-coded. A halted run renders as no comparison possible. The contradiction flag is null, not false. Couldn't check and checked and found nothing are different facts.

shot.concept: Figure 2 (ledger-table). self_report.py's ledger rendering with statuses color-coded (confirmed directly: 14 entries, OPEN/UNVERIFIED/RESOLVED/BY_DESIGN vocabulary), the live-unittest-discovery mechanism replacing the stale hard-coded '143 tests' claim, the generated caveat arrow from ledger entry to compare button, and the null-vs-false distinction as two contrasting chips.

beats.act: chapter 3a - checking the critique before building for it
beats.narration_text: Version two came from a sharper critique. The layout hides how each agent actually got there. I checked whether it was true. It was, and worse than stated. The comparison route makes exactly one EDGAR fetch. Not two. Both producers read different lenses over the identical data. They run sequentially, not concurrently. A tidy two-column layout would have invented a request and a concurrency that don't exist. So the layout renders the real shape. And the retry path, only ever observed before in scripted mock failures, now renders in the HTTP layer with real sequence numbers.

shot.concept: Figure 3 (one-fetch-not-two). The wrong, assumed symmetric two-column/two-fetch design struck through, replaced by the corrected four-band layout (setup / one shared spine / two agent columns / verdict), then the retry path rendered live with real sequence numbers -- the first time that path has been visible outside the test suite's scripted mock failures. TRIMMED (cut-to-6:00 guidance, item 2): the specific lookup_cik/fetch_company_facts millisecond timings named in the original draft are cut from narration and from this beat's on-screen content -- the one-fetch structural claim is the load-bearing fact, not the exact timing sample, and PEDAGOGY.md's runtime section explains why this was cut rather than the structural claim.

beats.narration_text: Every cited number traces back to that agent's own input. On the real Apple case, three hundred eighty-three point two six six billion dollars checks out. It reconciles to the raw fact, despite completely different formatting. The zero point three four debt-to-equity ratio doesn't. It appears nowhere in the input at all. That's a fabrication. Before this, finding it required a human reading a raw log by hand.

Two rows: a real reconciled figure ($383.266 billion checkmark against the raw fact Assets: 383266000000.0, despite completely different formatting) and the fabricated one (0.34, absent from input entirely), ending on a FABRICATION stamp -- the reel's central artifact, matching the cold open's own hook.

beats.act: chapter 4a - the refactor that was supposed to do nothing
beats.narration_text: Third session. Sixteen modules sat flat at the root. One of them shadowed a standard library module. Everything moved into layers: core, adapters, pipeline, datasources, producers, validation. Zero behavior change, verified two ways. The full suite passed after eight incremental moves. And the untested web server's route table, and the responses for nine calls, came back byte-identical after every edit.

Sixteen flat modules including the parser.py stdlib-shadow, the six-layer target architecture (core/adapters/pipeline/datasources/producers/validation), eight move-steps each with a green suite check, then the before/after route-and-response snapshot landing on '0 differences'.

beats.narration_text: Three duplications came out, each with a specific risk. The number-extraction regex existed three times, verbatim. Each copy asked the reader to keep it in sync by hand. A drifted copy wouldn't raise an error. It would just quietly report a claim it never verified.

shot.concept: Figure 6 (dedup-collapse). The number-extraction regex duplicated verbatim across claims.py/consistency.py/verification.py (confirmed directly: all three define the same pattern) collapsing into one shared module. TRIMMED (cut-to-6:00 guidance, item 1): the _latest_value cross-producer-import duplication case from the original draft is dropped entirely -- this beat now covers only the regex duplication, per the script's own explicit instruction to drop this case first when shortening.

all three collapse into one shared module, converging into a single box
caption: 'a drifted copy wouldn't error -- it would quietly report an unverified claim'

beats.narration_text: And forty-seven new tests. The one I care about is test_layering dot py. It reads the imports as a syntax tree. It fails if a layer reaches somewhere it shouldn't. A passing architecture test is worthless if it can't fail. So I broke it three times on purpose. Each violation named the offending file and line. Then I restored it.

shot.concept: Figure 7 (layering-violations). test_layering.py's AST-based import check, confirmed present with six real test methods, stress-tested by three deliberately introduced violations that each produce a named failure (file + line), then restored -- the reel's clearest 'a test that can fail' demonstration.

beats.narration_text: Which brings us back to the cold open. Seven of twelve tickers over-flag was prose. So all thirty-one real runs this system has ever stored became a versioned fixture. Each one is labeled. Each one was replayed through today's actual comparator, not hand-predicted. Sixteen of thirty-one are disjoint-concept false positives. Zero are genuine conflicts.

beats.narration_text: Here's the structural reason, the actual finding. Every flagged run pairs producer A's Assets, Revenues, and Net Income against producer B's Earnings Per Share and Operating Income. Those vocabularies never intersect, by design. The earnings producer's own docstring calls it deliberate. No amount of tuning can ever produce a genuine-conflict finding. You cannot detect disagreement between two witnesses asked different questions. The fix is upstream. It wasn't this session's job. Eight new tests assert it.

shot.concept: Figure 9 (disjoint-vocabularies). Producer A's concept list against Producer B's, with an empty intersection made visually explicit; the earnings producer's own docstring quoted verbatim (confirmed directly: 'deliberately disjoint from producers/financial.py's'); ends on the explicit scope boundary ('fix is upstream, not this session's job') plus the +8 tests count -- this reel's sharpest falsifiability beat, matching the cold-open's structural claim rather than a hypothetical edge case.

a gap diagram forms between the two lists, the intersection zone highlighted and empty
docstring quote chip: '…deliberately disjoint…'
caption: 'you cannot detect disagreement between two witnesses asked different questions'
chip: 'FIX IS UPSTREAM -- NOT THIS SESSION'S JOB' beside a second chip '+8 TESTS'

beats.act: chapter 6a - two things nobody had measured (the suppression)
beats.narration_text: Building that corpus surfaced two findings nobody had written down. First: replay the historic fabrication case, the one run that ever proved this tool catches something real. It wouldn't flag today. Two fixes shipped the same day back in August. One widened the regex. The other required both agents to have cited a number before flagging. In that run, producer B's side is empty. So the second fix suppresses the flag entirely. Neither fix is wrong on its own.

shot.concept: Figure 10 (two-fixes-one-record). The record card f4a4c782 (confirmed directly: named in self_report.py's asymmetry-fix-suppresses-historic-true-positive entry) reprised from the cold open, now shown in full: two same-day fixes converging on it, the both-sides-non-empty gate as the specific suppressing mechanism, ending restamped SUPPRESSED TODAY.

both fix chips send a line converging onto the record card
the record card desaturates to grey, restamped: 'SUPPRESSED TODAY'

beats.act: chapter 6b - the regex bug and the stale footnote
beats.narration_text: Second, a real extraction bug. The shared regex truncates a large comma-grouped number with no currency symbol down to its last digit group. An operating income of thirteen billion, nine hundred seventy-one million dollars extracts as the string zero zero zero point zero. Confirmed reproducing against today's code. Both went into the ledger as open issues. Neither is fixed.

shot.concept: Figure 11 (regex-truncation). '13,971,000,000.0' truncating to '000.0' under the bare-decimal fallback, confirmed reproducing against today's code (run 515f263a). beats.act: chapter 7a - the honest ledger, true now
beats.narration_text: True now that wasn't before this period. The interface calls the comparison route. It leads with the subsystem's own failures instead of a demo. The one-fetch, two-lenses design and the sequential execution are rendered honestly. The retry path is visible outside the test suite for the first time. A fabricated number is findable without reading a raw log by hand. The code sits in enforced layers. The enforcement is proven able to fail. The over-flagging claim is now a versioned corpus and eight executable tests, instead of a sentence. Two hundred twenty-four tests, up from one hundred sixty-nine, green at every step.

beats.act: chapter 7b - the honest ledger, still not true + uncommitted
beats.narration_text: Still not true. The comparison route, the trace module, and every line of JavaScript have zero automated tests. Everything in those first two sessions was verified by hand, in a browser. None of this week's UI work has ever been exercised against a real language model. No working Gemini key. No Ollama running here. Every verified claim in those sessions used a mock adapter or fixture data. The retry and halt path is still only observed against scripted mock failures, never a live model. The over-flagging isn't fixed. The suppressed true positive isn't resolved. That one needs a human judgment call, not a patch. The regex bug is still corrupting a real figure every time it's hit. Fourteen entries in the ledger now. Twelve of them are open or unverified. One is critical. That's up from eleven at the start of the period. Nothing was resolved this period. And the largest one: none of this is committed. The last commit in this repository predates all four sessions. Fifty-six changed or new files, sitting in a local working tree. That's not a technical risk I discovered. It's one this project already named after the previous period's check. Still true. Now bigger.

beats.narration_text: So here's the smallest true claim I can make about this week. The interface got honest. The code got layers. And the headline feature got measured, for the first time. The measurement says it has never once caught the thing it was built to catch. A tool that can't produce evidence against itself isn't a verification tool. It's a demo. Sixteen flags. Zero conflicts.
